1.pericope_label: Hear my prayer, O Lord: enter not into judgment, and the remembrance of the days of old

schools.summary: Augustine accepts the title and reads through it to another David, since past events were figures of things to come, and makes the appeal to righteousness a commendation of grace against those who impute their evil to God and their good to themselves.

Calvin agrees with the general opinion about the occasion and denies that righteousness here means merit or hire, making it the goodness that leads God to defend his people; Gill shows by inventory that nothing in a man would bear examining.

Henry has the psalmist explain his own plea as meaning the righteous promises of the gospel and not the threatenings of the law; Spurgeon describes the movement of the prayer as a change from one court to another, so that he cries hear my prayer rather than hear my suit.

Clarke accepts the inscription about the rebellion, reads the petition as a plea that God not come into court either as witness or as judge, and follows the darkness of the third verse into caves and tombs.

Ellicott divides faithfulness and righteousness between the covenant promise and the conviction that the Judge must do right, finds in these verses the paradox of the book of Job, and corrects two renderings; Keil and Delitzsch note the absence of the inscription from some codices and distinguish the later persecution psalms by their penitential character.

debates: To what righteousness does the psalmist appeal? Henry has him explain his own plea as the righteous promises of the gospel rather than the threatenings of the law, since by the broken covenant of innocency he would be undone; Calvin denies that the word speaks of merit or hire and makes it the goodness that moves God to defend his people; Augustine makes it a commendation of grace so that no one thinks his righteousness his own; Ellicott splits the pair between covenant promise and the certainty that the Judge must do right; Clarke turns the next verse into a plea that God not enter the court at all.

How can one prayer invoke justice and then shrink from it? Ellicott observes the sudden deprecation of the justice just invoked and finds here the paradox of the book of Job, where protestations of innocence alternate with dread of being taken at one word; Spurgeon describes it as a change of court, the suit turned into a petition; Gill reaches the same end by showing that nothing in a man would bear examining.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the psalms of the later persecution from those of the earlier by the deep melancholy into which the mourning of a dethroned king was turned by blending with the penitential sorrow of one conscious of his own guilt, and observe that this is why the church made this psalm the last of its seven penitential psalms.

Spurgeon reads the opening as a deliberate change of court, since the psalmist was inclined to lay his case before the bench of justice but chose instead to present it as a petition, and so asks that his prayer be heard rather than his suit.
themes: a plea for hearing and for answer
righteousness pleaded as promise not as desert
no living man able to stand at that bar
a soul darkened as among the long dead

7.pericope_label: Hear me speedily: the morning of lovingkindness, the way to walk in, and the land of uprightness

schools.summary: Henry hears haste in the opening and calls it the haste of vehement desire rather than of unbelief, and observes that those delivered from the pit may still look like men going down to it; Spurgeon answers that mercy has wings to its heels when misery is in extremity, and keeps the morning in the ear rather than the eye.

Gill places the prayer at night and reports two Jewish readings of the morning, takes the guidance as the doing of God revealed will and submission under affliction, and finds in the last verse an act of justice to the enemies that is an act of grace to the sufferer.

Clarke reads the whole passage off the flight, making the morning the hour when news might come and the way a literal road through country held by rebels, and quotes his old Psalter on the good Spirit leading into the right land; Wesley reduces the morning to seasonably and speedily.

Ellicott grants the dependence on earlier psalms and denies that it detracts from the reality of the feeling, allows the morning either sense, prefers that the good spirit lead rather than that the spirit is good, renders the promised country a level land, and takes the fleeing verb reflexively; Keil and Delitzsch trace each cry of this half to its model.

debates: Does the dependence on earlier psalms tell against this one? Keil and Delitzsch say the second half seems still more like a reproduction of the thoughts of earlier psalms and trace each cry to its model; Ellicott grants the dependence and denies the inference, holding that it does not detract from the reality of the feeling expressed by means of these ancient sobs and cries, and that the contrast with the former times just recalled makes the anguish the more intense.

What is the way in which he should walk? Clarke takes it literally of the road, since the rebels held all the country and the fugitive did not know which direction would avoid them; Ellicott makes it the way at once of duty and of safety; Gill makes it the doing of the revealed will of God and submission to it under affliction. On the country promised, Ellicott renders a level land taken metaphorically of tranquillity where Clarke keeps the place of safety.
outliers: Clarke reads the petition for guidance as a request for road directions in a country held by the enemy, asking that providence point out which way to go so as not to fall in with the rebels.
Clarke old Psalter renders the clause about the Spirit as a promise, that the good Spirit shall lead him into the right land.
themes: a night that waits for news
guidance sought for road and for duty
enemies cut off as an act of mercy
